decisions.reason: As a core airfield-lighting control product closely tied to the firm's installed-base business, it likely stays because even under uncertain airport spending its results should clear aspiration levels better than more peripheral offerings and it uses existing capabilities efficiently.

This surveillance display fits the firm's integrated airport-operations portfolio, so boundedly rational management would give it time and organisational slack rather than exit quickly while market demand remains noisy.

A broad airport-systems training program supports the established product base and service revenues, making it a relatively low-risk complement that management would usually retain unless performance clearly fell below aspirations.

This narrower training course appears more peripheral and easier to absorb into other service offerings, so if results lag aspirations management is likely to reallocate those resources to stronger core products and development projects.

Collaboration software directly matches the firm's stated direction toward integrated, real-time and data-driven airport operations, so management would likely tolerate short-run uncertainty and keep investing.

Because the multilateration system is presented as a flagship and is central to the firm's future surveillance positioning, management would be inclined to retain it and search for market traction before considering withdrawal.
